w: Built on the old Hovden sardine cannery site, this aquarium opened in October 1984 as the first to exhibit a living kelp forest and the first to keep a great white shark alive. Its biologists pioneered jellyfish husbandry, and in 1999 it launched Seafood Watch, the guide that reshaped sustainable seafood buying.
s: A sardine cannery reborn as a living kelp forest, 1984
_facts: Opened October 1984 on the former Hovden Cannery site
First aquarium to exhibit a living kelp forest
First aquarium to keep a great white shark alive on display
Launched the Seafood Watch sustainable-seafood guide in 1999

w: Built in 1791-94 as the Royal Presidio Chapel, this is the oldest stone building in California and the state's oldest continuously operating parish. It ranks among the oldest serving cathedrals in the US and is the only surviving presidio chapel in California -- the last piece of the original Monterey Presidio.
s: California's oldest stone building, a parish since 1794
_facts: Built 1791-1794 as the Royal Presidio Chapel
Oldest stone building in California
Only surviving presidio chapel in California
Oldest continuously operating parish in the state

w: First lit February 1, 1855, this is the oldest continuously operating lighthouse on the US West Coast. It still carries its original third-order Fresnel lens, was automated only in 1975, and remains an active Coast Guard aid to navigation, now ringed by a municipal golf course. Pacific Grove runs a small onsite museum.
s: West Coast's oldest working lighthouse, lit since 1855
_facts: First lit February 1, 1855
Oldest continuously operating lighthouse on the US West Coast
Retains its original third-order Fresnel lens
Automated in 1975; still an active Coast Guard aid to navigation

w: Once Ocean View Avenue, renamed for the 30-plus sardine canneries lining it by the early 1940s -- begun 1902, collapsed after the postwar sardine crash, last plant closing 1973. Steinbeck immortalized the row in his 1945 novel and 1954's Sweet Thursday. The old Hovden Cannery became the Monterey Bay Aquarium.
s: Steinbeck's sardine-cannery street, industry to tourism
_facts: Originally Ocean View Avenue; officially renamed Cannery Row in 1958
More than 30 canneries operated here at its early-1940s peak
Last cannery closed in 1973
Setting of Steinbeck's Cannery Row (1945) and Sweet Thursday (1954)

w: Four miles of Monterey Bay coastline carved from the shuttered Fort Ord army base, now a state park with a boardwalk, a beach path, and a four-mile road for walking and biking past exhibits on its military past. The dunes are nesting ground for sensitive species, so access stays limited to marked paths.
s: Army base dunes reclaimed, four miles of coastal trail
_facts: Created from part of the closed Fort Ord military base
Covers 4 miles of Monterey Bay coastline
Includes a boardwalk, beach path, and a 4-mile road for walking and biking
Dune nesting habitat limits access to marked paths and trails

w: Opened 1880, this resort sprawled over 20,000 acres of Monterey, Pacific Grove, Pebble Beach and Carmel Valley, with eight golf courses, polo grounds and a racetrack. Salvador Dali staged his 1941 party here, 'A Surrealistic Night in an Enchanted Forest.' Closed 1942; the Navy took it over in 1947.
s: A 20,000-acre resort where Dali threw a surreal party
_facts: Opened in 1880, closed in 1942
Grounds once included 8 golf courses, polo grounds, and a racetrack
Hosted Salvador Dali's 1941 party 'A Surrealistic Night in an Enchanted Forest'
US Navy purchased the property in 1947; later home to the Naval Postgraduate School

w: Built in 1827 by Mexican authorities, this is the oldest surviving government building in California and the state's first designated Historical Landmark. It marks where US Commodore John Drake Sloat raised the American flag in 1846, declaring California part of the United States.
s: Where the American flag first rose over California, 1846
_facts: Built in 1827 under Mexican rule
Oldest surviving government building in California
California's first designated Historical Landmark
Site where Commodore Sloat raised the US flag in 1846

w: Built originally for the YWCA, 16 of its buildings went up between 1913 and 1929 to designs by architect Julia Morgan -- 11 still stand. Sited on the Monterey Peninsula's western tip near old Moss Beach, the grounds sit on land recognized as the homeland of the Rumsen Ohlone people.
s: Julia Morgan's YWCA retreat on the Ohlone shoreline
_facts: Built for the YWCA between 1913 and 1929
16 buildings designed by architect Julia Morgan; 11 survive today
Located in Pacific Grove on the Monterey Peninsula's western tip
Recognized as Rumsen Ohlone homeland
